title: Indian Startup Vimag Labs Challenges China's Rare Earth Grip With Magnet-Free EV Motor
excerpt: Vimag Labs has patented a magnet-free EV motor technology, enhancing India's EV supply chain independence.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Vimag Labs has patented a magnet-free EV motor technology, enhancing India's EV supply chain independence.
  • The startup's software-defined motor matches conventional motors' performance without rare-earth elements.
  • Vimag Labs raised $5 million in Series A funding, partnering with vehicle manufacturers for pilot programs.
  • China dominates rare earth mining and processing, making Vimag's technology crucial for India's EV ambitions.

  • Bengaluru-based Vimag Labs has secured its fifth Indian patent for a Virtual Magnet Synchronous Motor that eliminates rare-earth permanent magnets from EV motors.
  • The startup's software-defined motor platform generates magnetic fields electronically, matching the performance of conventional permanent magnet motors without the supply chain vulnerability.
  • Vimag Labs raised $5 million in Series A funding led by Accel and is conducting pilot programs with two-wheeler and passenger vehicle manufacturers.
  • China controls roughly 60% of global rare earth mining and 90% of processing, making rare-earth-free motor technology a strategic priority for India's EV ambitions.

Bengaluru-based deep-tech startup Vimag Labs has secured its fifth Indian patent for a technology that could fundamentally reshape the electric vehicle supply chain: an electric motor that works without rare-earth permanent magnets.

The patent, titled "A Robust Rotating Transformer Excited Synchronous Motor and Its Control," covers the foundational architecture of the company's proprietary Virtual Magnet Synchronous Motor (VMSM) platform. Unlike conventional Permanent Magnet Synchronous Motors that rely on magnets embedded in the rotor — magnets made from rare-earth elements overwhelmingly sourced from China — Vimag's system generates and controls its magnetic field in real time using power electronics and proprietary software algorithms.

How the Technology Works

Traditional EV motors depend on permanent magnets made from neodymium and other rare-earth elements. These magnets create the rotating magnetic field that drives the motor. The problem: China controls approximately 60% of global rare earth mining and 90% of refining capacity, giving Beijing enormous leverage over the global EV supply chain.

Vimag's approach replaces these physical magnets with what the company calls a "virtual magnet." The rotor is excited wirelessly — without brushes or slip rings — while electronics and software continuously control the magnetic field. The result is a brushless synchronous motor that the company says matches or exceeds the performance of conventional permanent magnet solutions.

> **"Chara Technologies has developed Synchronous Reluctance Motors that eliminate permanent magnets altogether using redesigned rotors."**

"This patent is the outcome of over 87,600 engineering hours. It strengthens every dimension of our commercial roadmap — OEM partnerships, licensing, manufacturing scale-up, and future growth."

— Manish Seth, Co-founder and CEO, Vimag Labs

The Competitive Landscape

![Bengaluru — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/View_from_Visvesvaraya_Industrial_and_Technological_Museum_%282025%29_02.jpg/3840px-View_from_Visvesvaraya_Industrial_and_Technological_Museum_%282025%29_02.jpg)

Vimag is not the only Indian startup working to reduce reliance on rare-earth magnets. Chara Technologies has developed Synchronous Reluctance Motors that eliminate permanent magnets altogether using redesigned rotors. Conifer replaces expensive rare-earth magnets with cheaper ferrite magnets. Viridian Igni Propulsion is pursuing yet another approach.

What distinguishes Vimag, according to The Hindu BusinessLine, is that rather than redesigning the motor or substituting materials, it recreates the function of a permanent magnet electronically. This makes the motor "largely software-defined" — a characteristic that could make integration easier for automakers.

Funding and Commercialization

Founded in September 2025 by Manish Seth and Piyush Desai, Vimag Labs raised $5 million in its Series A round led by Accel, with participation from Chakra Growth Fund and Thinkuvate. The company, which operates under the Volektra brand, has development centers in India, Germany, the US, and Poland.

The technology has reached technology readiness level seven — meaning it has been demonstrated in an operational environment — and the company is conducting pilot programs with established two-wheeler and passenger car manufacturers. Expansion is planned into light commercial vehicles and high-power industrial systems in the 200-600 kW range, along with applications in robotics, defense, and cooling systems.

Vimag has also signed a manufacturing agreement with Jendamark Pvt. Ltd. to support production scale-up. Its intellectual property portfolio now includes five granted patents, ten in the pipeline, and fifteen trademarks covering motor architecture, software controls, and power electronics.

Strategic Implications for India

For India, the technology directly supports the Make in India and Atmanirbhar Bharat objectives by enabling indigenous development of critical electric motor technology. As the country pushes to electrify its transportation sector, dependence on Chinese rare-earth supplies represents a strategic vulnerability that homegrown alternatives could help address.

For OEMs, Vimag's platform offers a dual advantage: lower motor costs and freedom from rare-earth supply chain risks. The company says its solution is designed as a plug-and-play system that automakers can integrate without major changes to existing production lines.
